talks.title: Teuta Hyseni - Keynote: Expect the Unexpected
talks.teaser: Examines teuta Hyseni - Keynote: Expect the Unexpected and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Teuta Hyseni delivers the BSides Prishtina keynote on expecting the unexpected, reflecting on Kosovo's first BSides and her journey from Kosovo to international cybersecurity roles.

Key Topics: BSides Prishtina as proof of vibrant Kosovo cybersecurity youth; increasing ransomware and nation-state cyber warfare; AI and IoT expanding attack surfaces; and even household appliances as hackable targets.

Technical Details: Hyseni connects global trends—ransomware, cyber warfare, AI, autonomous vehicles, and IoT—to local implications for Kosovo's emerging security community, noting even refrigerators run exploitable applications.

Takeaways: Cybersecurity challenges are universal regardless of geography. Regional BSides events like Prishtina build local communities connected to global threat landscapes.

talks.title: Kastriot Fetahaj - 0Keyboard (a simple keyboard with the evil inside)
talks.teaser: Reviews kastriot Fetahaj - 0Keyboard (a simple keyboard with the evil inside) and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Project Concept

Kastriot Fetahaj presents 0Keyboard: a cheap USB keyboard hiding a Raspberry Pi Zero W running Kali Linux and the open-source P4wnP1 framework for red-team and physical penetration tests.

Hardware Build

Components include a wired keyboard, USB hub, Pi Zero, microSD, and rewired USB data/power lines. He strips the hub, splices microcontroller and hub cables, isolates metal shielding with tape to avoid shorts, and reassembles a normal-looking device.

Software Stack

Kali provides the base OS; P4wnP1 adds a web UI to configure Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB gadget modes, and attack modules without custom firmware development.

Attack Capabilities

The implanted Pi can perform keystroke injection, network or Bluetooth scanning, USB mass-storage exfiltration, and remote control over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. A demo diagram shows a phone operator triggering injected keystrokes on a connected Windows host.

talks.title: Chris Davis - LeXSS - Bypassing Lexical Parsing Security Controls
talks.teaser: Presents chris Davis - LeXSS - Bypassing Lexical Parsing Security Controls and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
HTML lexical parsing

Bishop Fox's Chris Davis introduces LeXSS: bypassing sanitizers when you have HTML injection but not direct XSS. Browsers tokenize HTML into RCDATA, raw text, plain text, or executable data states; attackers want the dangerous data state for script execution.

Namespaces and double parsing

Parsers also handle MathML and SVG namespaces with different rules. WYSIWYG editors parse input twice—browser first, then editor sanitizer—creating a mismatch attackers exploit by crafting payloads the browser parses differently than the sanitizer.

Real exploits

TinyMCE and Walla payloads nest textarea/iframe or iframe/comment/math wrappers so sanitizers treat malicious content as safe text. After re-parsing, JavaScript executes in the DOM. Similar parser-differential issues appear in DOMPurify-related cases. Success requires per-editor parser quirks and lexical confusion.

talks.title: Isuf Deliu - Ransomware-as-a-Service: demystifying a multi-billion dollar industry
talks.teaser: Presents isuf Deliu - Ransomware-as-a-Service: demystifying a multi-billion dollar industry and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Ransomware as an Industry

Isuf Deliu, a KPMG incident-response and threat-intelligence consultant, demystifies ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS). He frames modern ransomware as a multi-billion-dollar criminal industry—not lone hackers in basements—but organized operations with corporate structure.

## Threat Intelligence Lens

Deliu advocates CTI-informed defense: understanding attacker economics, tooling, and TTPs improves every security function from training to detection and pen testing. Ransomware is the case study for why context beats generic controls.

## The RaaS Org Chart

RaaS operators function like software companies: development teams build and evade AV, QA tests payloads, HR handles recruitment and time off, finance manages payments, and affiliates rent the platform for a revenue share. Affiliates conduct intrusions while operators maintain the malware and infrastructure.

## Double Extortion Reality

Modern campaigns encrypt and exfiltrate data, so paying ransoms no longer guarantees deletion. Deliu's goal is to help defenders and leaders see ransomware as a business they must out-plan—not a mysterious black box.
